title: Informal Conjecture (polynomial expansion and bounded twin-width)
statement_text: All classes of polynomial expansion may also have bounded twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is defined via contraction sequences $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$, where $G_{i-1}$ is obtained from $G_i$ by contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices; for $u\in V(G_i)$ let $u(G)$ be the set of vertices of $G$ contracted into $u$, and let $uv$ be a red edge of $G_i$ if the pair $u(G),v(G)$ is not homogeneous in $G$ (neither all edges nor no edges between them). The twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that some contraction sequence has red degree at most $d$ in every $G_i$ (twin-width 0 graphs are exactly the cographs). A class has bounded expansion if there is a function $f$ such that every $r$-shallow minor (minor obtained by contracting disjoint connected subgraphs of radius at most $r$ and deleting vertices and edges) of a graph in the class has edge density at most $f(r)$, and polynomial expansion if $f$ can be taken polynomial. The authors show that proper minor-closed classes (which have polynomial expansion) have bounded twin-width, and remark that, as far as they know, all classes of polynomial expansion may also have bounded twin-width. Bounded twin-width is incomparable with bounded degree, bounded expansion and nowhere denseness: cubic graphs have unbounded twin-width while cliques have twin-width 0. In their concluding questions they ask whether classes with polynomial expansion have bounded twin-width and, if so, whether contraction sequences can be computed efficiently, announcing as a first step that $t$-subdivisions of $n$-cliques have bounded twin-width if and only if $t=\Omega(\log n)$.
notes: Stated in hedged prose ('as far as we know … may also'); clearly conjectural but no labelled environment.
paper_title: Twin-width I: tractable FO model checking

title: Question (common superclass for FPT FO model checking)
statement_text: Do bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes admit a natural common superclass still admitting an FPT algorithm for FO model checking?
context_text: Twin-width is defined via contraction sequences $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$, where $G_{i-1}$ is obtained from $G_i$ by contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices; for $u\in V(G_i)$ let $u(G)$ be the set of vertices of $G$ contracted into $u$, and let $uv$ be a red edge of $G_i$ if the pair $u(G),v(G)$ is not homogeneous in $G$ (neither all edges nor no edges between them). The twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that some contraction sequence has red degree at most $d$ in every $G_i$ (twin-width 0 graphs are exactly the cographs). FO model checking asks, given a first-order formula $\varphi$ and a graph (or binary structure) $G$, whether $G\models\varphi$; it is FPT on a class if solvable in time $f(|\varphi|)\cdot|G|^{O(1)}$. A class is nowhere dense if for every $r$ some graph is not an $r$-shallow minor of any member. FO model checking is FPT on bounded-degree graphs, graphs of locally bounded treewidth, $H$-minor-free graphs, classes of (locally) bounded expansion and finally nowhere dense classes (Grohe, Kreutzer and Siebertz). The authors prove that it is FPT on classes of bounded twin-width, given a contraction sequence witnessing it; this covers non-sparse classes such as bounded rank-width graphs, map graphs, $K_t$-free unit ball graphs, posets with antichains of bounded size and $d$-dimensional grids. Bounded twin-width is incomparable with nowhere denseness (even with structurally nowhere dense classes, i.e. FO transductions of nowhere dense ones), and in their Hasse diagram of classes with FPT FO model checking the two roughly subsume all current knowledge; the question is whether there is a natural common superclass of both on which FO model checking is still FPT.
notes: Posed as a rhetorical question in the caption of Figure 3, not in a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Twin-width I: tractable FO model checking
